evidence.note: Faced with many compile errors (missing methods, borrow-checker, type mismatches), it chose to rewrite from scratch rather than patch one-by-one — a structural decision, but about code-writing hygiene, not compiler design falsification.

Repeatedly oscillates between heredoc, Python generator, base64 encoding, and line-by-line writing to dodge escaping/brace issues, returning to methods that already failed — churn without a decisive, effective fix.

Correctly diagnoses the root cause (Python raw strings truncated by ''' sequences in Rust char literals causing brace imbalance) yet keeps hitting the same failure afterward rather than adopting a robust once-and-for-all remedy.

The same root cause (duplicate/imbalanced code from re-appending) recurs ~6 times; each time it applies the same local fix (truncate to last balance-0 point, re-add) without changing the fundamentally fragile approach.

Trajectory ends still mechanically closing impl blocks; never reaches a working build or the 780-test run where genuine design-falsification (type info, sized ops, struct layout) would surface — no design pivot observed.

reasoning: The agent's adaptation is confined to the source-writing mechanism, where the same root cause (escaping/brace imbalance) recurs constantly and is met with local fixes and ineffective method-swapping rather than a decisive structural correction — matching the anchor-3 pattern of 'resists structural change even when the same root cause recurs,' but weaker because the pivots oscillate back to already-failed approaches (pulling toward 0). Because it never reaches a working compiler or test feedback, there is essentially no evidence of the design-level revision (type representation, codegen strategy, IR) this dimension targets. I place the observed level at 2: some recognition of dead ends and occasional root-cause diagnosis, but no effective, converging correction and no compiler-design pivot.
